source_text: Πρὸς τούτοις δὲ θαυμάσαι ἄν τις, πόθεν ἐπῆλθε τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ, ὡς λέγουσιν οἱ κακολογοῦντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν, μὴ ἑωρακόσιν αὐτὸν ἀναστάντα ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν μηδὲ πεισθεῖσιν ὅτι θειότερόν τι ἦν ἐκεῖνος, πρὸς τῷ μὴ φοβηθῆναι τὰ αὐτὰ τῷ διδασκάλῳ παθεῖν καὶ ὁμόσε χωρῆσαι τῷ κινδύνῳ καὶ καταλιπεῖν τὰς πατρίδας ὑπὲρ τοῦ διδάξαι κατὰ τὸ Ἰησοῦ βούλημα τὸν παραδοθέντα αὐτοῖς ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγον. οἶμαι γὰρ ὅτι ὁ εὐγνωμόνως ἐξετάζων πράγματα οὐκ ἂν λέγοι τούτους ἑαυτοὺς παραδεδωκέναι περιστατικῷ βίῳ ἕνεκεν τῆς Ἰησοῦ διδασκαλίας χωρίς τινος μεγάλης πειθοῦς, ἣν ἐνεποίησεν αὐτοῖς διδάσκων οὐ μόνον διακεῖσθαι κατὰ τὰ μαθήματα αὐτοῦ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλους διατιθέναι, καὶ διατιθέναι προὔπτου ὄντος ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἀνθρώπων βίον ὀλέθρου τῷ τολμῶντι πανταχοῦ καὶ πρὸς πάντας καινοτομεῖν καὶ μηδένα ἀνθρώπων, ἐμμένοντα τοῖς προτέροις δόγμασι καὶ ἔθεσι, φίλον ἑαυτῷ τηρεῖν. ἆρα γὰρ οὐχ ἑώρων οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ, τολμῶντες οὐ μόνον Ἰουδαίοις ἐκ τῶν προφητικῶν λόγων παριστάνειν ὅτι οὗτος εἴη ὁ προφητευθεὶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἔθνεσιν ὅτι ὁ χθὲς καὶ πρώην σταυρωθεὶς ἑκὼν τοῦτον τὸν θάνατον ὑπὲρ τοῦ τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένους ἀνεδέξατο, ἀνάλογον τοῖς ἀποθανοῦσιν ὑπὲρ πατρίδων ἐπὶ τῷ σβέσαι λοιμικὰ κρατήσαντα καταστήματα ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας; εἰκὸς γὰρ εἶναι ἐν τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους καὶ δυσλήπτους τοῖς πολλοῖς λόγους φύσιν τοιαύτην, ὡς ἕνα δίκαιον ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ ἀποθανόντα ἑκουσίως ἀποτροπιασμοὺς ἐμποιεῖν φαύλων δαιμονίων, ἐνεργούντων λοιμοὺς ἢ ἀφορίας ἢ δυσπλοΐας ἤ τι τῶν παραπλησίων. λεγέτωσαν οὖν οἱ βουλόμενοι ἀπιστεῖν τῷ Ἰησοῦν ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων ἀποτεθνηκέναι τρόπῳ σταυροῦ, πότερον οὐδὲ τὰς Ἑλληνικὰς παραδέξονται καὶ βαρβαρικὰς πολλὰς ἱστορίας περὶ τοῦ τινας ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ τεθνηκέναι καθαιρετικῶς τῶν προκαταλαβόντων τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὰ ἔθνη κακῶν· ἢ ἐκεῖνα μὲν γεγένηται οὐδὲν δὲ πιθανὸν ἔχει ὁ νομιζόμενος ἄνθρωπος πρὸς τὸ ἀποθανεῖν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει μεγάλου δαίμονος καὶ δαιμόνων ἄρχοντος, ὑποτάξαντος ὅλας τὰς ἐπὶ γῆν ἐληλυθυίας ἀνθρώπων ψυχάς; ὁρῶντες δὲ ταῦτα οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ καὶ ἄλλα τούτων πλείονα, ἃ εἰκὸς αὐτοὺς ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μεμαθηκέναι, ἔτι δὲ καὶ δυνάμεώς τινος πληρωθέντες. ἐπεὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς μένος καὶ θάρσος οὐ ποιητική τις παρθένος ἀλλ᾿ ἡ ἀληθῶς φρόνησις καὶ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ, (ἔσπευσαν,) ἵν᾿ ἔκδηλοι μετὰ πᾶσιν οὐ μόνοις Ἀργείοις γένοιντο ἀλλὰ καὶ πᾶσιν Ἕλλησιν ὁμοῦ καὶ βαρβάροις, καὶ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄροιντο.
pass_a_gloss: One would also marvel at from where the disciples of Jesus came to, as those who speak evil of Jesus say, not having seen him risen from the dead nor being persuaded that he was something divine, to the point of not fearing to suffer the same things as their teacher and to share in the danger and to leave their homelands for the sake of teaching according to Jesus' will the word delivered to them by him. For I think that one examining things with gratitude would not say that they handed themselves over to a precarious life for the sake of Jesus' teaching without some great persuasion, which he worked in them by teaching, not only to live according to his teachings but also to set others in order, and to set in order, even if it means rushing forward as one who dares to innovate everywhere and before all people, and not to consider any person, remaining in the former doctrines and customs, a friend. Did the disciples of Jesus, then, not see, daring not only to present to Jews from prophetic words that he was the one prophesied, but also to the other nations that the one crucified the day before and previously willingly accepted this death for the sake of the human race, analogous to those who die for their homelands to extinguish pestilential powers or plagues or difficulties? For it is likely that in the nature of things, according to certain unspeakable and hard-to-believe words to the many, there is such a nature that one righteous person, having died voluntarily for the common good, would avert the evil demons, which work plagues or pestilences or difficulties or something similar. Let those who wish to disbelieve that Jesus died for humans on a cross say, then, whether they will not also accept the many Greek and barbarian histories about some people having died for the common good, abolishing the evils that had taken hold of cities and nations, or whether those things have come to pass but the man thought to have died for the abolition of a great demon and the demons ruling, having subjected all the souls of humans who have come upon the earth, is not believable. Seeing these things and many more, which it is likely they learned from Jesus in secret, and also being filled with some power, since he gave them courage and confidence, not from some created maiden but from the true wisdom and intelligence of God, they hastened to become manifest to all, not only to Argives but also to all Greeks and barbarians together, and to gain good fame.
pass_b_english: One would also be astonished to consider the source of the disciples' conviction, given what the critics of Jesus allege. They say the disciples had not seen him risen from the dead, nor had they been persuaded that he was something divine. Yet they did not fear suffering the same fate as their teacher; they embraced the danger, abandoned their homelands, and dedicated themselves to teaching the message he had entrusted to them, in line with his will. I believe that anyone examining these matters fairly would not claim the disciples surrendered themselves to such a precarious existence for the sake of Jesus' teaching without a powerful persuasion at work within them. He instilled this conviction by teaching them not only to order their own lives according to his lessons, but to set others in order as well—to do so even if it meant pressing forward boldly as innovators before all people everywhere, refusing to regard as a friend anyone who clung to the old doctrines and customs.

Did the disciples of Jesus not see clearly? They dared not only to demonstrate to the Jews from the prophetic writings that he was the promised one, but also to proclaim to the other nations that the man crucified just days before had willingly accepted that death for the sake of the human race. Their claim was analogous to those who die for their homelands to extinguish pestilential forces, plagues, or famines. For it is plausible that the nature of things operates according to certain unspeakable and hard-to-grasp principles: that one righteous person, dying voluntarily for the common good, can avert the evil demons who cause plagues, pestilences, famines, or similar disasters.

Let those who refuse to believe that Jesus died for humanity on a cross answer this: will they not also accept the many Greek and barbarian histories that tell of individuals who died for the common good, abolishing the evils that had seized cities and nations? Or will they admit those stories happened, yet insist that the man thought to have died for the abolition of a great demon and the ruler of demons—the one who had subjected all human souls that have come upon the earth—is somehow not credible? The disciples saw these parallels, and many more besides, which they likely learned from Jesus in private. Moreover, they were filled with a power, since he gave them courage and confidence—not from some created maiden, but from the true wisdom and intelligence of God. Thus they hurried to become manifest to all people, not only to the Argives but to all Greeks and barbarians together, and to win an honorable reputation.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering of the clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate English version that preserves the agency, modality, and theological distinctions (e.g., 'not from some created maiden but from the true wisdom and intelligence of God'). All arguments regarding the disciples' motivation and the comparison to Greek/Barbarian histories are fully represented.

The translation accurately reflects the Greek text, with appropriate citations and adherence to the source. No errors were found in the translation, and all elements of the source are preserved in the English version.
